title: Dates are the export crop that ships Tunisia's scarce blue water abroad: exports grew about sixfold from 2000 to 2022 on the crop with the highest blue water footprint per tonne among Tunisia's main crops and a low return per m3

rootCauses.cause: State investment in water mobilisation, generous on-farm irrigation incentives and supported irrigation water prices expanded irrigated agriculture (SRC-TG-864); our reading, not stated by the source, is that this made expansion profitable without pricing the scarcity of the water used. The national agricultural studies centre calls exports from irrigated agriculture one of the major justifications for irrigated agriculture
Government-built groundwater infrastructure in the south, followed by tolerated private palm extensions from the 2000s, expanded the irrigated date area beyond planned oases
With irrigation water prices supported, farmers' choices follow return per hectare rather than per m3, and dates have a high return per hectare despite a low return per m3

dataGaps: Blue water footprint of dates after 2010: three estimates were opened (5,000 m3/t blue for 1981-2010, SRC-TG-860; 3,270 m3/t blue for 1996-2005, SRC-TG-868; about 2,900 m3/t total implied for 2013 exports, SRC-TG-861). No estimate after 2013 was found.

Blue virtual water exported through dates for a recent year: no published figure after 2013. Applying the per-tonne estimates to 2022 exports (130,307 t) would give roughly 430-650 million m3 of blue water, but this mixes periods and is not a published estimate. The 2013 published value is 283.6 million m3 (total, for 97.8 kt; FAOSTAT records 105,803 t of date exports in 2013).

The OTE report (SRC-TG-744) live URL was unreachable on 2026-11-21; its 60% export share was confirmed verbatim by the source-verifier against the Wayback Machine copy (December 2020 report), but it is an NGO figure without a stated method.
Irrigated olive area and the blue water exported through olive oil today: SRC-TG-860 gives 39% irrigated olive production for 1981-2010; no recent figure was opened.
Export incentives specific to dates (FOPRODEX transport support, investment code advantages for export agriculture): found only in press reports, not in an official text, so not used.
Farm income per m3 for date farms against alternative crops in the southern oases: only national 1996-2005 averages (SRC-TG-868).

Crop-level projection of date area, exports or embedded water under water constraints: none found. The forward-looking sources are a sector-level CGE model (SRC-TG-866) and the farm income projection for Kebili traditional oases in sibling record FND-TG-742; neither projects export volumes.
author: TahaGHZ
excerpt: Olive oil and dates dominate Tunisia's agricultural exports: together they were 45% of agricultural export value in 2010. Of the two, dates depend most on blue water: - they are fully irrigated; - they have the highest…

sections.heading: Problem
Root causes
Evidence
sections.content:
- **Water footprints, 1981-2010 average (AquaCrop):** dates 650 m3/t green, 5,000 blue, 5,600 total; olives 7,100 green, 420 blue, 7,500 total; tomatoes 140 green, 180 blue, 320 total (SRC-TG-860, Table 5).
- **Water footprints, 1996-2005 (Mekonnen and Hoekstra model):** dates 1,030 green, 3,270 blue, 80 grey, 4,390 total m3/t. Dates and olives together make up 47% of the crop blue water footprint (SRC-TG-868). This source comes from the same research group as SRC-TG-860 but uses a different model and period, so it is only partly independent.
- **Trade is not explained by water scarcity.** Over 1981-2010, blue water scarcity did not explain net virtual water trade for any of the six main crops. For dates, each extra 1,000 ha of irrigated land raised net virtual water export by 5.6 Mm3 (SRC-TG-860). The authors note that the reason lies outside their variables, such as agricultural policies, the value of water and international prices (SRC-TG-860).
- **Share of virtual water exports.** Olive oil, dates, wheat and tomatoes made up 72% of crop-related virtual water export over 1996-2005, 68% for olive oil alone (SRC-TG-860).
- **2013 export flows.** Exports of 145,900 t of olive oil and 97,800 t of dates carried 1,079.6 and 283.6 million m3 of virtual water, and more than 80% of exported virtual water was blue (SRC-TG-861). FAOSTAT records 105,803 t of date exports for 2013, so the implied water per tonne is approximate.
- **Production and area.** Dates rose from 105,000 t (2000) to 174,000 t (2010) and 369,000 t (2022), all official FAOSTAT figures (SRC-TG-862). Harvested area was 31,610 ha in 2000 (official). FAOSTAT area flags are official for most years up to 2016 (61,240 ha), except 2010 and 2012. From 2017 they are imputed or estimated (SRC-TG-862).
- **Area sources disagree.** The ministry figure relayed by ONAGRI is 57,385 ha in 2022, of which 38,000 ha in Kebili (SRC-TG-743). FAOSTAT imputes 77,404 ha for 2022, about 35% higher (SRC-TG-862). The ministry figure is preferred for the level; both are recorded.
- **Export share sources disagree:**
  - 35% in 2022, from our FAOSTAT calculation (SRC-TG-862, SRC-TG-863);
  - 36.1% in 2021 and a 2011-2021 average of 44.4%, from ONAGRI (SRC-TG-743);
  - 60%, from an NGO report (SRC-TG-744), checked against the Wayback Machine copy because the live URL was unreachable; no method is given.
- **Exports in tonnes and value.** 22,411 t (2000), 84,282 t (2010), 130,307 t (2022), 129,929 t (2023). Export value was US$38.6 million in 2000 and US$256.7 million in 2023 (SRC-TG-863).
- **Sources disagree on the water content of dates and of the export basket.** For dates, the estimates are:
  - 5,600 m3/t total, 5,000 blue (SRC-TG-860);
  - 4,390 m3/t total, 3,270 blue (SRC-TG-868);
  - about 2,900 m3 per exported tonne, implied by the 2013 figure (SRC-TG-861).

  For olive oil, SRC-TG-860 finds olives mostly green water (7,100 green against 420 blue m3/t). SRC-TG-861 calls olive oil the most water-demanding commodity at 7 m3/kg "due to the need of blue water for its processing". The studies use different methods (AquaCrop, a global model, farm surveys) and periods. All values are recorded; none is preferred.
- **Projection.** A sector-level CGE model (conference paper, not peer-reviewed) projects:
  - agricultural output 7.39% to 19.87% lower by 2050 under 5-14% less water availability;
  - lower agricultural exports.

  It names dates, olive oil, tomatoes and citrus as the main export products, and cites yield declines of 2% per year for tomatoes and dates over 2021-2050 (SRC-TG-866). It does not project the crop mix, so this record stays `current`.

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- **Water:** dates draw on the southern aquifers. SRC-TG-864 describes intensive use of "near-fossil" water and illegal extensions in Kebili. Aquifer overdraft itself belongs to the water lane; this record covers only the crop and export choice.
- **Energy:** borehole pumping in the oases uses energy, but no figure was opened for this topic (none sourced).

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- Crop water allocation by virtual water content and bioclimatic zone, as proposed in SRC-TG-861 and SRC-TG-864 ("import water-intensive products, export low-water high-value ones").
- Programme national d'économie d'eau en irrigation (PNEEI), evaluated by SCET Tunisie 2016 (cited in SRC-TG-864).
- Water use efficiency scenarios (network rehabilitation, irrigation modernisation, less water-intensive varieties) modelled in SRC-TG-866.
- FOPRODEX export transport support (Fonds de promotion des exportations), seen in press only.
- Higher charges for blue water in export value chains, suggested in SRC-TG-861.
- Expanding irrigation only for crops with high water productivity and a large irrigated-versus-rainfed land productivity gap, suggested in SRC-TG-868.

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content:
Date and tomato footprints, returns per m3 and per ha, production and area, and the ONAGRI and virtual-water indicators were traced to the cited copies. The FAOSTAT trade file (SRC-TG-863) was opened directly as the original bulk file.

**Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Checked: SRC-TG-860 Table 5 p. 291 and discussion p. 295; SRC-TG-868 water footprint text, Table 8 (dates blue EWP 0.11, column alignment inferred from text extraction) and Table 9 text; SRC-TG-864 sections on water demand, mobilisation, exports and typology; SRC-TG-862 FAOSTAT QCL rows (dates production and area, 2000, 2010, 2022); SRC-TG-863 FAOSTAT TCL bulk file, rows Tunisia / Dates / Export quantity (22,411 t in 2000, 130,307 t in 2022, flag A) and Export value (256,663 thousand US$ in 2023); SRC-TG-743 Figure 11 and indicator table; SRC-TG-861 abstract and section 4; SRC-TG-740 section 2; SRC-TG-866. Corrections: root cause 1 "official justification" reworded to "one of the major justifications" (SRC-TG-864); the "without pricing the scarcity" causal chain labelled as our reading; tomato blue footprint "50-180 m3/t" corrected to 180 m3/t blue (SRC-TG-860). Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

resolvedSources.title: Oasis extension trajectories in Kebili territory, southern Tunisia: drivers of development and actors' discourse
resolvedSources.publisher: New Medit (CIHEAM), vol. 21 n. 5, 2022; authors Mekki I., Ferchichi I., Taouajouti N., Faysse N., Zairi A.; doi 10.30682/nm2205f
resolvedSources.extracts:
Introduction:

> "The government supported the development of groundwater use infrastructures to revitalize ancient oases and to develop a few modern oases (Côte, 2002; Mekki et al., 2013). The government, however, had no clear plans for the future of palm grove areas in the Kebili region (Brochier-Puig, 2004). Still, farmers were not allowed to drill individual boreholes on their own outside traditional oases to limit the use of the aquifers. Despite this lack of vision, palm grove developments took place, especially from the 2000s onwards, in areas locally referred to as "extensions". In 2020, the production of dates in these extensions represented approximately 85% of the date production in the region and 80.7% of national date production (CRDA, 2020). Collectively, these extensions are currently the largest illicit agricultural area based on groundwater use in Tunisia."

Section 3.1.1 "Growth in planted areas":

> "The first oasis survey carried out by the Ministry of Agriculture in 1976 revealed that the total area of date palm oases in Kebili was around 5,240 ha. As private extensions were not recognized by the administration, they were not counted until the end of the 1990s. The results of the survey conducted by the Ministry of Agriculture between 1994 and 1996 and reported by Kassah (1996) showed that the area of the extensions reached 7,000 ha by then. [...] Figure 3 shows the evolution of extension areas based on Kebili CRDA (2010 and 2016), and our estimate for 2020 (32,700 ha)."

> "The annual average rate of increase over the three periods 1996-2010, 2010-2016 and 2016-2020, is 540 ha/year, 2073 ha/year and 1434 ha/year, respectively. [...] In comparison with extensions, the pace of development of legal oases is rather low and stable. Legal oases covered around 8,315 ha in 1996 and did not exceed 10,485 ha in 2018."

Section 3.1.2 (typology, Northern and Southern Douz districts only):

> "[...] (7.23%), bordering extensions covered 1,645 ha (15.83%) and disconnected extensions 7,991 ha (76.93%)." (mutakhma extensions 751 ha)

Section 3.2 "Factors that triggered the pioneering front":

> "First, farming in ancient oases became less profitable due to land fragmentation and a decrease of land fertility because of the loss of biodiversity. Moreover, there were water deficits in traditional oases, and pumped water flows had been decreasing. In particular, artesian wells, which were numerous in the area, had all dried out by the early 2000s. Second, market liberalisation of the date palm sector led to an increase of the price of Deglet Noor dates."

> "In the mid-1980s, low-cost drilling techniques became easily available in the Kebili region. Illegal boreholes were drilled in the new extensions created in the periphery of old oases. [...] There were also public subsidies for building cold warehouses for the conservation of Deglet Noor dates inside and outside ancient oases. Owners of cold warehouses took advantage of their legal access to electricity to provide energy to boreholes located in extension areas. Later, from 2014 onwards, farmers started using solar power [...] In total, 2358 solar panels were detected in the Kebili region"

> "They also reported that, with the exception of 500 ha of new oases created by the PDES, only a few oases had been developed by the administration. A manager commented that: "sometimes we regret not having created new irrigated oases in collective lands; at least they could have been irrigated from collective and public wells and we would have avoided all these illicit drillings.""

> "Before the revolution, Kebili CRDA had better control over illegal borehole drilling and had more legitimacy to act. In 2011, thousands of boreholes were created, and the CRDA was unable to intervene."

Section 3.3.1 "Intense groundwater use and its consequences":

> "Available estimates suggest the number of illicit boreholes in extensions increased from several dozen in the 1970s to 1,500 in the 1990s, 3,500 in 2010 (Gharbi, 2010) and to 9,678 in 2017 (CRDA, 2018)."

Section 3.3.2 "Actors' discourse about causal relationship between extension development and overexploitation of groundwater resources" (what interviewed CRDA staff members said):

> "Interviewed CRDA staff members underlined that the main threat to sustainability of agriculture in Kebili region was decreasing water resources. [...] From the 2000s, water started to become scarce and the impacts of these "nearby" extensions on ancient oases were clearly perceptible. They led to reduced water resource availability within these oases. The intense exploitation of deep aquifer has also resulted in an increase of groundwater levels in shallow aquifers, which has caused drainage problems."

Section 3.4 "Limited attempts to manage palm grove extensions":

> "At the end of the 1980s, after the intervention of the Nefzaoua and APIOS projects, the administration formally integrated certain groups of extensions that were in continuity with the ancient oases into the water turn of collective networks [...] However, a continuous decline in administrative surveillance and control of illegal drilling, as well as applying sanctions was reported by Kassah (1996)."

> "A visit by a government delegation in the Kebili region in 2017 led to an initiative to legalise mutakhma extensions. At the time, private farms inside the moutakhma extensions covering around 3750 ha were legalised and were provided subsidies."

> "In July 2021, in cooperation with the AFA, a new attempt was made to legalise extensions by creating irrigated public areas."

> "Apart from the mutakhma extensions, farmers within other type of extensions do not have access to either water saving or soil protection subsidies. Farmers created drainage networks without any idea about their real effectiveness."

Discussion:

> "By contrast, in Tunisia, the government chose to consider these activities as illegal, but at the same time chose not to act to limit the extension of groundwater-based agriculture"

Additional extracts (sections 3.2-3.4):

> "Interviewed administration representatives acknowledged the limitations of ancient oases. They underlined the inefficient management of collective irrigation networks and the lack of maintenance of networks created by farmers in the mutakhma extensions."

> "A staff member mentioned that "In some places, the CRDA felt obliged to give permission to access electrical energy even if it had doubts about the intentions of the farmers [in terms of creating new palm groves outside official areas]. The CRDA has thus played a role in accelerating the development of extensions and illegal drillings.""

> "A decrease in the piezometric levels of 24.70 m has also been observed at Smida oasis between 1991 and 2020 (average of 1.18 m decreases per year)."

> "[...] and that in the extension area "the salinity of the shallow water table has become very high in the last 5 years and exceeds 5 g/l." Farmers from the Blidette extension highlighted the effect of photovoltaic panels that were installed on the aquifer in 2015. Farmers rarely stopped pumps connected to these panels, which has led to increased use of groundwater."

> "These subsidies were mainly water saving (drip irrigation; basins) and soil protection (the sandy amendment) equipment. However, subsidies to moutakhma extensions were later put on hold due to a lack of a legal basis for this new initiative. In 2018, Kebili CRDA announced a plan to provide subsidies to all other extensions, but this was later also put on hold."

Abstract: "These private initiatives, called "extensions", have developed on collective unfarmed areas outside historical oases."
resolvedSources.notes: Peer-reviewed. Many figures are relayed from Kebili CRDA reports and databases (CRDA 2010-2020, CRDA 2018 inventory) that we did not open; the 2020 extension area (32,700 ha) is the authors' own estimate from Google Earth imagery 1984-2020. Internal inconsistency: extensions at 85% of Kebili output cannot equal 80.7% of national output when Kebili is about 73% of national output (SRC-TG-742); the 80.7% figure is not used as an indicator. The 751 / 1,645 / 7,991 ha typology covers only the Northern and Southern Douz districts, not the whole governorate. Actor quotations are interview material.

resolvedSources.notes:
Official ONAGRI sheet, undated (latest data 2022, some marked as estimates). The PDF's two-column table was extracted with labels and values offset; the mapping above was made line by line and should be re-checked against the PDF by the verifier, in particular the order of the four indicators 9.9% / 15.7% / 44.4% / 12.1% (TCAM of export value 2010-2021 = 9.9%, consistent with SRC-TG-742). The 68.2% Deglet Nour share uses the same 2018 oasis survey as SRC-TG-742, which gives 72.3%; the difference is not explained.
Denominator caveat: the 32.4% / 65.1% / 1.2% shares divide 2018 survey areas (18,590 / 37,387 / 677 ha) by the 2022 DGPA total of 57,385 ha; on the 2018 survey total of 56,654 ha they would be 32.8% / 66.0% / 1.2%.

resolvedSources.title: L'exportation des dattes et le coût hydrique des devises : des politiques agricoles qui vouent la région de Kébili à la pénurie
resolvedSources.publisher: Observatoire Tunisien de l'Economie (OTE); Z. Vernin with M. Helali
resolvedSources.extracts:
Section I(c) (ligatures restored from the PDF text, which drops "ti" and "tt"):

> "En effet, la Deglet Nour a fait l'objet d'une spéculation agricole sous l'effet de l'économie du marché. Très prisée sur les marchés internationaux, la production de Deglet Nour a été d'abord promue par l'Etat, et cette orientation a été ensuite suivie et dépassée par le secteur privé au rythme des extensions licites et en particulier illicites."

> "Aujourd'hui la Deglet Nour représente d'ailleurs 80% des exportations de dattes tunisiennes. Cette tendance est d'ailleurs toujours actuelle puisque 94% des plantations d'âge inférieure à 5 ans sont des palmiers Deglet Nour."

English gloss: Deglet Nour was first promoted by the state, then the private sector followed and overtook it through licit and especially illicit extensions; Deglet Nour is 80% of date exports and 94% of plantations younger than 5 years.

Section III(b) (market structure):

> "Dans cette filière et malgré les prix plancher (ou « prix référentiel à la station ») fixés par le Groupement Interprofessionnel Fruits, les producteurs ne disposent que d'un faible pouvoir de négociation avec le collecteur qui intervient en premier lieu."

> "Kébili produit environ 150 000 tonnes de dattes par an, soit plus de 60% des dattes en Tunisie. Dans le gouvernorat, 15% seulement de la production régionale peut être stockée. 13 unités de conditionnement sur 75 sont à Kébili, et représentent 15% des emplois dans cette branche 5 exportateurs de dattes sur 65 sont à Kébili, et exportent à peine 10% de la production régionale directement depuis Kébili."

English gloss: despite GIFruits floor prices, producers have little bargaining power with collectors; Kebili produces about 150,000 t (over 60% of national output) but can store only 15%, hosts 13 of 75 packing units and 5 of 65 exporters, and exports barely 10% of its output directly.

Introduction:

> "La culture dattière a pris de l'ampleur et de la valeur à mesure que ce se sont développées les exportations qui atteignent aujourd'hui 60% de la production totale des dattes"

English gloss: exports now reach 60% of total date production.

Additional extracts (Section I(c)):

> "C'est le PDES qui en réhabilitant et en créant des oasis, a commencé à introduire massivement la variété Deglet Nour [...] En effet, les opérations de rénovation, au-delà des infrastructures hydrauliques, ont pu aussi consister à arracher des anciens palmiers de variétés communes pour les remplacer par la Deglet Nour dans les années 1970-1980."

English gloss: the Southern Water Master Plan (PDES), by rehabilitating and creating oases, began introducing Deglet Nour on a large scale; renovation works in the 1970s-1980s sometimes uprooted old common-variety palms to replace them with Deglet Nour.

> "Elle représente une importante source de revenus et notamment de devises, pouvant se vendre au plus du double du prix que la majorité des variétés communes sur le marché local comme international."

English gloss: Deglet Nour can sell at more than twice the price of most common varieties on local and international markets.

> "L'orientation vers la Deglet Nour s'est donc faite au détriment des 150 autres variétés locales de dattes qui existent en Tunisie."

English gloss: the shift to Deglet Nour came at the expense of the 150 other local date varieties in Tunisia.
resolvedSources.notes:
NGO policy report, tier B, with an explicit critical stance. Most figures are relayed from secondary sources we did not open: the 94% young-plantation figure is footnoted to the Ministère de l'environnement et du développement durable 2015 oasis monograph; the 80% export share carries no footnote; the storage and packing-unit figures cite the same MEDD 2015 monograph (footnotes 83-84); footnotes 86-88 on packer and exporter counts were not checked. Other references include APII 2017 and Khamassi 2015 (GIZ/IDEE value chain report). The 60% export share conflicts with ONAGRI's official export effort of 36.1-50% over 2011-2021 (SRC-TG-743). Climate projections in the report (footnote 76) are relayed from the MEDD 2015 monograph and are not used here.
Access: on 2026-11-21 the live URL refused connections during source verification; the text was checked against the Wayback Machine copy (web.archive.org/web/2024id_/<url>, 31 pages, December 2020).

resolvedSources.title: Virtual water trade patterns in relation to environmental and socioeconomic factors: A case study for Tunisia
resolvedSources.publisher: Science of the Total Environment 613-614 (2018) 287-297; authors Chouchane H., Krol M.S., Hoekstra A.Y.; doi 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2017.09.032
resolvedSources.extracts:
Abstract (p. 287):

> "The results show that NVWI during the study period for the selected crops is not influenced by blue water scarcity. NVWI correlates in two alternative models to either population and precipitation (model I) or to GDP and irrigated area (model II). The models are better in explaining NVWI of staple crops (wheat, barley, potatoes) than NVWI of cash crops (dates, olives, tomatoes)."

Section 2 (p. 288), crop selection:

> "for Tunisian export (olives and dates, which together account for 45% of the total agricultural export value in 2010; FAOSTAT, 2015), and the two crops with highest economic blue water productivity in the country (tomatoes and potatoes; see Chouchane et al., 2015). Wheat and barley are mainly rain-fed and net imported. Olives are rain-fed and dates are mainly irrigated. Both tomatoes and potatoes are mainly irrigated, while tomatoes are exported to a little extent and potatoes are mainly imported (Ministry of Agriculture, 2011)."

Table 1 (p. 288), average 1981-2010 (columns: production 10^3 t/yr; % irrigated production; net import 10^3 t/yr; economic blue water productivity US$/m3):

> "Olives 720 | 39 | -100 | 0.03"
> "Dates 95 | 100 | -30 | 0.11"
> "Tomatoes 690 | 100 | -2.2 | 1.13"
> "Potatoes 250 | 98 | 30 | 0.97"
> "Wheat 1100 | 22 | 1100 | 0.12"

Section 2.2 (p. 290):

> "The export of olive oil, dates, wheat and tomatoes accounts for 72% of the total crop-related virtual water export (68% for olive oil only) over the period 1996-2005 (Chouchane et al., 2015)."

Table 5 (p. 291), average WF per unit of crop, m3/tonne, 1981-2010 (green | blue | total):

> "Olives 7100 | 420 | 7500"
> "Dates 650 | 5000 | 5600"
> "Tomatoes 140 | 180 | 320"
> "Wheat 4100 | 550 | 4700"

Section 3 (p. 291-292):

> "net virtual water exports related to cash crops (olive oil, dates and tomatoes) are increasing as well."

> "In model II, an increase in irrigated land by 1000 ha increases the net virtual water export of dates by 5.6 Mm3."

Discussion (p. 295):

> "Dates and olives, the most exported crops in Tunisia, have the highest total WF per unit among the selected crops. Dates have the highest blue water footprint in m3/tonne. Additionally, dates are only produced in the south of Tunisia, the region with the highest scarcity level (Chouchane et al., 2015). A remaining question is why a water-scarce country continues producing a blue water intensive crop like dates for export. The selected variables of this study couldn't answer this question; other factors must be the reason. Dates have also a low economic water productivity and from an economic perspective reallocating the water used by dates for growing other crops, with higher water productivity, such as potatoes and tomatoes would be more beneficial (Chouchane et al., 2015)."

> "there are other factors that could influence the virtual water trade in a country that are not included in current study, such as: agricultural policies, value of water, international prices, etc."
resolvedSources.notes: AquaCrop-based water footprints, six crops, 1981-2010. Excludes grey water. Water availability from Ministry of Agriculture data without environmental flows. Data period ends 2010; date area and exports have grown strongly since (see SRC-TG-862, SRC-TG-863). Economic blue water productivity values come from Chouchane et al. (2015), not recomputed here; they match the 1996-2005 "blue EWP in irrigated agriculture" column of Chouchane et al. (2013) Table 8 (SRC-TG-868), so they are 1996-2005 values even though Table 1 is headed 1981-2010.

resolvedSources.title: Quantification of Virtual Water balance of Tunisia: Flows Embedded in the main produced, consumed and exchanged Agricultural Commodities
resolvedSources.publisher: New Medit (CIHEAM) n. 2/2017, pp. 11-18; authors Makhlouf M., Frija A., Chebil A., Souissi A., Stambouli T., Benalaya A.
resolvedSources.extracts:
Abstract (p. 11):

> "Our calculations show that Tunisia is a net virtual water "importer". We also surprisingly show that, even though olive production is mostly rain fed, olive oil production is still identified as the most water-demanding commodity (7 m3/kg) in Tunisia due to the need of blue water for its processing. By exporting 145.9 thousand tons of olive oil and 97.8 thousand tons of date in 2013, Tunisia has respectively lost 1079.6 and 283.6 Million m3 of virtual water. On the other hand, by importing 2146.6 thousand tons of cereals and 15.7 thousand tons of potato in the same year, Tunisia has respectively saved 2901.7 and 3.14 Million m3 of water resources."

Résumé (p. 11, French version of the abstract):

> "Nos calculs montrent que la Tunisie est un pays "importateur net " d'eau virtuelle."

English gloss: Our calculations show that Tunisia is a net importer of virtual water.

Section 4 (results, p. 14-15):

> "Unlike grain, the blue virtual water content of vegetable represents around 60% of the total virtual water content due to a couple of reasons such as the period of cultivation which is summer wherein the crop water requirement is the highest"

> "The results obtained show that, more than 80% of the virtual water exported is blue virtual water."

Section 5 (discussion, p. 16-17):

> "Results show that commodities such as olives, almond, oats and barley are among the crops with higher share of green water content compared to the share of blue water (Chouchane et al., 2013). Most of these crops are not traded (exported) and are consumed locally. Concerning virtual water trade, our results show that Tunisia is essentially exporting blue water. This is especially due to the high contribution of water intensive crops such as dates and olive oil to the agricultural export of Tunisia."

Conclusion (p. 17):

> "Finally, it was also shown that Tunisia is a net importer of virtual water. But we believe this is not intentional and is simply due to its dependency from international markets for the import of many necessary food commodities such as cereals, animal feeds, and vegetable oils."
resolvedSources.notes: Based on the authors' field surveys across bioclimatic zones (single year 2013 for trade flows). The numeric values of Table 1 (virtual water content by crop, including irrigated maltaise citrus and irrigated tomato) and Table 2 could not be extracted: the PDF uses an embedded font whose glyphs do not map to text. The claim that olive oil is 7 m3/kg "due to the need of blue water for its processing" conflicts with SRC-TG-860, which puts olives at 7,100 m3/t green and 420 m3/t blue; the two studies use different methods and system boundaries. Implied blue+green content of exported dates in 2013 is about 2,900 m3/t (283.6 Mm3 / 97.8 kt), lower than the 5,600 m3/t total (5,000 blue) in SRC-TG-860. FAOSTAT records 2013 date exports as 105,803 t (SRC-TG-863), not the 97.8 kt used in the paper, so the implied per-tonne value is approximate.

resolvedSources.title: FAOSTAT Crops and livestock products (QCL), Tunisia: area harvested and production of dates, tomatoes, watermelons, oranges, strawberries, olives
resolvedSources.publisher: FAO Statistics Division (FAOSTAT), bulk file Production_Crops_Livestock_E_Africa.csv
resolvedSources.notes: Production figures for 2022 are flagged official (A) and are the latest official year for most crops; 2023 values are imputed. Several area series are unreliable and should not be used: olives 2020 (3.6 Mha, estimated, larger than Tunisia's olive area), oranges 2020 (5,214 ha imputed, half the adjacent years), watermelon area (falls 80% from 2000 to 2023 while output rises 59%). Strawberry production is flat at about 10,000 t for two decades and estimated/imputed after 2020, which conflicts with the rapid growth of strawberry area reported for Cap Bon (SRC-TG-867); treat it as unknown. Date area flags are official (A) for 2000, 2009, 2011 and 2013-2016, imputed for 2010 and 2012, and imputed or estimated from 2017 onwards; the 2022 imputed value (77,404 ha) is about 35% above the ministry figure of 57,385 ha relayed by ONAGRI (SRC-TG-743). Orange production nearly doubles between 2017 (186,900 t) and 2018 (346,000 t), both official; this may be a series break, so long-run comparisons of orange export shares should be read with care.

resolvedSources.title: FAOSTAT Crops and livestock products trade (TCL), Tunisia: export quantity and value of dates, olive oil, tomatoes, tomato paste, watermelons, oranges, strawberries; wheat imports
resolvedSources.publisher: FAO Statistics Division (FAOSTAT), bulk file Trade_CropsLivestock_E_Africa.csv
resolvedSources.notes: Fresh tomatoes and processed tomato products (paste, peeled) are separate items; tomato paste is reported here in product weight, with no fresh-equivalent conversion. FAOSTAT trade is reported by calendar year, while Tunisian date and citrus campaigns run across years, so values differ from ONAGRI campaign figures.

resolvedSources.title: Évaluation de l'approvisionnement alimentaire dans un contexte de pénurie d'eau dans la région NENA. Application de l'approche courbe de coût d'approvisionnement alimentaire. Cas de la Tunisie
resolvedSources.publisher: FAO, prepared by Centre National des Études Agricoles (CNEA), Rome; ISBN 978-92-5-130826-4
resolvedSources.extracts:
Summary (p. xx):

> "En tant que pays manquant fondamentalement de ressources hydriques, la Tunisie a intérêt à importer le maximum possible de produits agricoles consommateurs d'eau afin de compenser ses déficits internes alimentaires et hydriques, tout en exportant des produits agricoles à faible consommation d'eau et de haute valeur ajoutée."

English gloss: As a country fundamentally short of water, Tunisia has an interest in importing as many water-consuming agricultural products as possible to offset its internal food and water deficits, while exporting agricultural products with low water use and high added value.

Summary (p. xviii):

> "La demande moyenne actuelle en eau par hectare réellement irrigué est estimée à 4 500 m³. Il est à remarquer, cependant, que cette demande est assez variable selon les cultures et les zones climatiques: elle peut se réduire à 1 000 et 2000 m³/ha pour les céréales et fourrages au nord et atteindre 15 000 à 20 000 m³/ha pour les palmiers dattiers dans les oasis du sud."

English gloss: Average water demand per actually irrigated hectare is about 4,500 m3; it ranges from 1,000-2,000 m3/ha for cereals and fodder in the north to 15,000-20,000 m3/ha for date palms in the southern oases.

Introduction (p. 1):

> "Entre 1956 et 2015, le taux de mobilisation des ressources hydrauliques est passé de 8 à 90 pour cent, le nombre des grands barrages s'est accru de 3 à 34, les puits de surface ont vu leur nombre multiplié par 46 et les sondages par 11 et les superficies irrigables estimées à environ 65 000 ha en 1956 (irrigués presque totalement à partir de puits de surface et de sources naturelles) dépassent 496 000 ha en 2015. Ce potentiel de production agricole indéniable permet à la Tunisie d'être autosuffisante en fruits et légumes et contribue largement à l'équilibre de la balance alimentaire du pays par les exportations qui représentent plus de 30 pour cent des exportations agricoles totales."

English gloss: Between 1956 and 2015 water mobilisation rose from 8 to 90%, large dams from 3 to 34, surface wells x46, boreholes x11, and irrigable area from about 65,000 ha (1956) to over 496,000 ha (2015). This makes Tunisia self-sufficient in fruit and vegetables, and irrigated exports are over 30% of total agricultural exports.

> "L'accroissement soutenu des superficies irrigables bénéficiant de grands investissements dans la mobilisation de l'eau, les nombreuses incitations financières très généreuses pour l'équipement à la parcelle et la politique de soutien des prix de l'eau d'irrigation a largement contribué à la sécurité alimentaire du pays."

English gloss: Sustained growth of irrigable area, backed by large investment in water mobilisation, very generous financial incentives for on-farm equipment and support to irrigation water prices, contributed greatly to the country's food security.

Section 2.8.7 (p. 67), irrigated agriculture in exports:

> "Les exportations: l'examen des données portant sur les exportations agricoles montre que la part de l'agriculture irriguée dans cet agrégat est relativement importante. Cette part est estimée, comme le montre le tableau suivant à 24 pour cent des exportations agricoles et agroalimentaires en 1995. Cette part a augmenté pour se situer à 33 pour cent de ce même agrégat en 2010 et à 29 pour cent en 2014. Cette contribution constitue en réalité l'une des justifications majeures de l'agriculture irriguée."

English gloss: Irrigated agriculture's share of agricultural and agri-food exports was 24% in 1995, 33% in 2010 and 29% in 2014; this contribution is one of the main justifications for irrigated agriculture.

Table 29 (p. 67), totals only, 1000 DT. Total agricultural and agri-food exports: 1995 462 000; 2000 628 000; 2005 1 225 600; 2010 1 647 800; 2014 2 048 800. Total irrigated agriculture exports: 108 700; 133 700; 265 900; 541 500; 589 600. Share (%): 24; 21; 22; 33; 29. Source line: "MARHP, annuaire statistique agricole 2012 et budget économique 2015".

Section 2.8 (p. 73), Table 33, water valorisation with and without the national irrigation water-saving programme (PNEEI), source SCET Tunisie 2016. Columns: water valorisation (DT/m³), water charges / total charges, water productivity (kg/m³):

> "Maraîchage — Avec PNEEI 1,098 14,1% 5,251; Sans PNEEI 1,234 13,4% 3,483"

> "Les résultats sont plus contrastés en maraîchage. Parmi les cultures qui ont les plus forts rendements, la tomate de saison et l'oignon d'été sont également celles qui valorisent le moins bien l'eau, au contraire du piment primeur."

English gloss: Results for vegetables are mixed. Among the highest-yielding crops, seasonal tomato and summer onion give the lowest value per m3, unlike early-season pepper.

Section on allocations (p. 54):

> "Ainsi, l'allocation moyenne à l'hectare passerait d'environ 4 700 m³/ha dans les années 2010 à 4 050 m³/ha à l'horizon 2030. L'allocation totale au secteur serait ainsi revue de 2 140 Mm³/an en 2010 à 2 035 Mm³/an en 2030."

English gloss: The average allocation per hectare would fall from about 4,700 m3/ha in the 2010s to 4,050 m3/ha by 2030; total allocation to the sector would go from 2,140 Mm3/yr in 2010 to 2,035 Mm3/yr in 2030.

Typology of irrigated perimeter groups (p. 139-140):

> "3. Le groupe des périmètres de types «Cap Bon»: il est caractérisé par des périmètres privés assez importants et des systèmes agrumicoles et maraîchers relativement développés mais aux dépens d'une surexploitation des ressources en eaux souterraines. Des programmes de sauvegarde des périmètres privés ont été engagés grâce aux transferts des eaux du Nord."

English gloss: Cap Bon-type perimeters have large private perimeters with well-developed citrus and vegetable systems, but at the cost of groundwater overexploitation. Safeguard programmes for private perimeters were launched using transfers of northern water.

> "4. Le groupe des périmètres de la Tunisie Centrale: il se distingue par un secteur irrigué privé assez dynamique mais au prix de la surexploitation des ressources phréatiques."

English gloss: Central Tunisia perimeters have a dynamic private irrigated sector, at the price of overexploiting shallow groundwater.

> "6. Le groupe des périmètres du Sud (Oasis maritimes, Oasis continentales, périmètres du Sud-est): Il se caractérise par l'exploitation intensive des eaux quasi fossiles dans les oasis et l'extension parfois illicite de celles-ci dans certaines zones (Kébili). La valorisation de l'eau sur le plan économique y est encore faible en raison de la tendance vers la monoculture du palmier dattier (filière dattes développée) et une consommation d'eau des plus élevées (15 000 à 20 000 m3/ha)."

English gloss: Southern perimeters rely on intensive use of near-fossil water and sometimes illegal oasis extensions (Kebili). Economic water value is still low because of the trend toward date palm monoculture and very high water use (15,000-20,000 m3/ha).
resolvedSources.notes: Report by the national agricultural studies centre (CNEA) for FAO. In Table 29 the per-crop rows (dates, citrus, fruit and vegetable derivatives, vegetables) are defective in the PDF: their values repeat those of Table 28 (milk, potatoes, sugar) and do not sum to the stated totals, so only the totals and the share line are used. Page numbers are printed page numbers (roman for the summary). The 2030 allocation figures come from DGEDA/MARH "Eau 21" updates cited in the report.

resolvedSources.title: Water Scarcity and Improved Water Use Efficiency in Tunisia: A Computable General Equilibrium Analysis
resolvedSources.publisher: Economic Research Forum (ERF) 31st Annual Conference paper; authors Mili M., Dhif M.A., Chekki H. (LEGI, École Polytechnique de Tunisie)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Abstract (p. 1):

> "Using a recursive dynamic Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model, we analyse the effects of four water-related hypotheses on GDP growth, social welfare, and trade balance by 2050."

> "The findings underscore the urgent need for practical actions to conserve water resources and highlight the importance of negotiating trade agreements that prioritize low-water-requiring products while managing the import of more water-intensive goods."

Introduction (p. 2):

> "Studies, such as [Yilmaz et al., 2023], suggest that changing climate conditions will further compromise both the quality and quantity of Tunisia's water resources, with projected annual average yield declines from 2021 to 2050 of 2% for tomatoes and dates, 0.5% for olives, and 0.2% for wheat."

Scenarios (p. 7): "H1: 5% reduction in water availability by 2050." "H2: 10% reduction in water availability by 2050." "H3: 14% reduction in water availability by 2050."

Results (p. 8-9):

> "The agricultural sector, as the largest consumer of water in Tunisia, experiences the most significant impact, with a projected 19.87% decrease in production levels by 2050 under the water scarcity hypothesis (H3), compared to the hypothetical situation (H0) without water constraints."

> "The long-term impacts are substantial, with decreases ranging from 7.39% (H1) to 19.87% (H3) depending on the level of water availability reduction."

Results (p. 10):

> "With regard to sectoral exports, simulation outcomes indicate that water constraints negatively affect agricultural exports by 2050."

> "According to the Tunisian Ministry of Agriculture, [MAGRHP, 2023a], Tunisia's primary exports in terms of agricultural and food products include olive oil, dates, tomatoes, tomato-based products, and citrus."
resolvedSources.notes: Conference working paper, not peer-reviewed; treat as tier B. The CGE model works at sector level (agriculture, food processing), not crop by crop, so it gives no projected crop mix. The crop yield trends (-2%/yr tomatoes and dates) are quoted from Yilmaz et al. (2023), which was not opened. Page numbers are the paper's own numbering.

resolvedSources.title: Water footprint of Tunisia from an economic perspective (Value of Water Research Report Series No. 61)
resolvedSources.publisher: UNESCO-IHE Institute for Water Education, Delft; authors Chouchane H., Hoekstra A.Y., Krol M.S., Mekonnen M.M.
resolvedSources.extracts:
Summary (p. 5):

> "At national level, tomatoes and potatoes were the main crops with relatively high economic water productivity, with a Tunisian average of 1.08 and 0.87 US$/m3 respectively, while olives and barley were the main crops with relatively low productivity, of 0.03 and 0.04 US$/m3 respectively. In terms of economic land productivity, oranges had the highest productivity, with 4040 US$/ha, and barley the lowest, with 130 US$/ha."

Section 3 (p. 13):

> "Dates, almonds, figs and grapes are the biggest blue water users with 3270, 1950, 1740 and 1080 m3/ton respectively."

> "The total blue WF is dominated by dates and olives (together 47%) and, to a lesser extent grapes, wheat and almonds."

Table 4 (p. 14), "The average green, blue and grey water footprint of main crops in Tunisia (1996-2005)". Columns: total WF (Mm3/yr) green | blue | grey | total; WF per ton (m3/ton) green | blue | grey | total; source Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011a):

> "Dates 110 350 10 470 | 1030 3270 80 4390"
> "Olives 7270 270 30 7570 | 8790 330 40 9150"
> "Tomatoes 50 40 10 100 | 60 50 10 120"

Table 8 (p. 19), "Physical and economic water productivity of main crops in Tunisia at national level (1996-2005)". Economic water productivity columns (US$/m3): total (green) EWP in rain-fed | green EWP in irrigated | blue EWP in irrigated | total EWP in irrigated | average EWP in irrigated and rain-fed; producer price US$/kg precedes them:

> "Dates ... 1.01 | 0.40 0.62 0.11 0.23 0.23"
> "Tomatoes ... 0.12 | 1.26 1.03 1.13 1.07 1.08"
> "Potatoes ... 0.21 | 0.80 0.77 0.97 0.88 0.87"

p. 19:

> "In terms of total ELP, oranges, tomatoes and dates had the highest ELPs, with 4040, 3770 and 3080 US$/ha respectively, while barley and olives had the lowest ELPs, with 130 and 170 US$/ha respectively."

p. 20:

> "Dates and oranges had relatively low economic water productivities (0.23 and 0.58 US$/ m3 respectively) as compared to potatoes (0.87 US$/ m3) (see Table 8), but the ELPs for dates and oranges were higher (3080 and 4040 US$/ha respectively) than the ELP for potatoes (2870 US$/ha)."

> "At a national level, the figures on economic water productivities (Table 8) provide little basis for understanding or explaining current cropping patterns. The figures on economic land productivities give a better basis for understanding, because various of the crops with large production volumes (especially tomatoes, potatoes, oranges and dates) have a relatively high ELP."
resolvedSources.notes: Research report from the same group as SRC-TG-860 (Chouchane et al. 2018), so it is only partly independent. It uses the Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011) global model for 1996-2005, whereas SRC-TG-860 uses AquaCrop for 1981-2010. It gives a lower blue water footprint for dates (3,270 m3/t against 5,000 in SRC-TG-860). The economic blue water productivities quoted in SRC-TG-860 Table 1 (dates 0.11, tomatoes 1.13, potatoes 0.97 US$/m3) are the "blue EWP in irrigated agriculture" values of Table 8 here, for 1996-2005, not 1981-2010 averages. Not peer-reviewed (report series), so tier B.

relatedItems.title: Irrigated fresh tomatoes, watermelons and citrus are grown almost entirely for the home market (about 2.4-4.1% exported in 2022), and agricultural policy as assessed by the World Bank in 2014 was biased against exports, so export promotion is not the main driver of their water use
